headline: Funding flows. Rockets explode. Geospatial warfare intensifies.
deck: This week saw a mix of funding rounds, explosive tests, and military applications of spatial data.

stories.head: True Anomaly raises $190M for co-orbital security
stories.body: True Anomaly secured $190 million in a Series C funding round, focusing on co-orbital security and space domain awareness. The funding is a clear signal that the Department of Defense is keen on enhancing its capabilities in this area, as evidenced by the recent influx of defense contracts. With a valuation now at $1.6 billion, True Anomaly is positioning itself as a key player in a rapidly growing market.
stories.soWhat: The defense pull-through here suggests that even in space, cash flow trumps pure tech innovation—investors want to see tangible military applications.

stories.head: Blue Origin's New Glenn rocket explodes during test
stories.body: A Blue Origin New Glenn rocket exploded during a hotfire test at Cape Canaveral, reminding everyone that not all tests go as planned. This incident raises questions about the reliability of the rocket, which is crucial for its upcoming missions. With SpaceX dominating the launch market, Blue Origin's setbacks could further delay its entry into the competitive landscape.
stories.soWhat: In a market where reliability is paramount, this explosion may set Blue Origin back in the race against SpaceX, which is already a few laps ahead.

stories.head: Spatial data weaponized in US-Iran conflict
stories.body: The use of spatial data as a weapon in the ongoing US-Iran conflict underscores the blurring lines between military and civil applications. As both sides leverage geospatial intelligence, companies providing this data are likely to see increased demand. The geopolitical implications of this trend could reshape how nations approach conflict in the digital age.
stories.soWhat: As maps become battlefields, firms in geospatial tech may find themselves on the front lines, raising the stakes for their products and services.

watchlist.title: Keep an eye on Bellatrix and TelePIX

watchlist.title: Watch for Anduril and L3Harris partnership
watchlist.body: Their tactical SDA constellation bid could signal a new wave of collaboration in defense tech.

watchlist.title: Monitor GPS jamming trends
watchlist.body: With jamming returning to pre-2024 levels, expect implications for both military and commercial aviation.

watchlist.title: Follow Palantir's TITAN program extension
watchlist.body: The $480 million extension indicates continued confidence in Palantir's capabilities in military applications.

talent.statLabel: Job orders YoY · plus 2 starters per head, an 8-year first
talent.head: Demand has doubled. So has our hit rate.
talent.body: EVONA's job orders are up 2.0× year-over-year, and for the first time in our eight-year history we're placing two new starters per EVONA staff member. The first number says demand is real. The second says we're converting it, which in recruitment is the only number that actually matters. Growth is heaviest in Series B/C startups; primes are running flat. Compensation isn't the variable. The constraint is schedule risk in the primes: senior engineers leave Boeing, Lockheed, Northrop because they want to ship hardware before retirement.
